top.title: Scientists find 10 different diets linked to slower aging
top.summary: A study by DZNE finds that healthy eating is associated with slower biological aging—and that there is more than one way to eat healthily. The researchers examined ten dietary patterns considered healthy, including the Mediterranean, Nordic, and a plant-based diet, as well as the DASH diet, which is designed to help lower blood pressure. The findings are published in the journal Nature Communications.
top.text: A large study involving approximately 7,500 people suggests that eating a healthy diet may help slow biological aging, and there is no single eating plan that stands above all others. Scientists at the German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases (DZNE) investigated 10 different dietary patterns, including the Mediterranean, Nordic, plant-based, and DASH diets. The DASH diet was specifically developed to help reduce blood pressure. Every dietary pattern examined was associated with slower biological aging, as measured by chemical changes in DNA that reflect the body's aging process. The findings were first identified using data from DZNE's Rhineland Study and then independently confirmed in another population. The research was published in Nature Communications . "Our study suggests that healthy eating goes hand in hand with slower biological aging. The effects are not massive, but they are measurable and relevant for prevention. By slowing the aging process, the risk of age-related diseases such as dementia or cardiovascular disorders can be reduced. Thus, healthy eating contributes to healthy aging," says Prof. Monique Breteler, Director of Population Health Sciences at DZNE and head of the Rhineland Study. "Importantly, there is probably no single 'correct' diet. According to our data, various dietary patterns are associated with slower aging, some more, some less. That is an encouraging finding, because it leaves room to tailor healthy eating to personal and cultural preferences, budget and taste." To investigate the connection between diet and aging, the scientists analyzed dietary information and blood samples from roughly 7,500 men and women. The initial analysis included 6,470 participants in DZNE's Rhineland Study in Bonn, Germany. The researchers then tested their findings using data from another 1,034 people enrolled in the EPIC-Potsdam Study, conducted by the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbrücke (DIfE). Rather than relying only on participants' chronological ages, the team looked for molecular signs of aging in their blood. Specifically, they measured DNA methylation, a process involving chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity and influence how cells function. These chemical patterns change in relatively predictable ways as people grow older, allowing scientists to estimate biological age. Unlike chronological age, which simply measures how long someone has been alive, biological age offers clues about how the body is aging at the molecular level. "We applied three different approaches, so-called epigenetic clocks, to read biological aging from DNA methylation," explains Juliana Tavares, a doctoral researcher at DZNE and lead author of the current publication. "To this end, we leveraged state-of-the-art technology, which allowed us to cover about 850,000 sites in the DNA. This is roughly twice as many as in most previous studies." The next step was to determine how closely each participant followed the 10 dietary patterns. Researchers compared reported food consumption with the recommendations for each diet and assigned scores reflecting how well individuals followed those guidelines. Because the diets emphasize different foods and nutritional goals, a person could receive a high score for one eating pattern while scoring poorly on another. In fact, participants who met one definition of healthy eating often did not meet the requirements of other diets. "One and the same person could therefore rank high on one diet score and low on another. In other words: People who ate healthily by one standard were often not the same people who ate healthily by another. According to our data, hardly anyone counts as a healthy eater by every standard at once," says Tavares. Despite those differences, the overall pattern was remarkably consistent. Better adherence to every one of the 10 diets was associated with slower biological aging. Some eating patterns showed stronger associations than others, but the absolute differences were relatively small. "While there are measurable differences between the diets, they are modest in absolute terms. It's the big picture what matters," says Tavares. "In summary: When it comes to slowing down the aging process, there isn't just one healthy diet, but indeed a whole repertoire of possible diets with a positive effect." One unexpected result emerged when researchers examined the association between diet and aging among smokers. The link between healthier eating and slower biological aging was stronger in smokers than in nonsmokers, even though smokers did not generally have healthier diets. The researchers have not yet determined what biological processes might explain this difference. One possibility is that the extensive damage caused by smoking leaves greater room for measurable improvements associated with healthier eating. However, the finding does not lessen the well-established dangers of tobacco use. "Smoking is very harmful to health," says Tavares, "One explanation for our findings might be that there is just more health benefit to gain for smokers by eating healthy because of the enormous detrimental effects of smoking." The scientists also investigated which biological processes might connect the different diets to slower aging. Although each eating pattern was associated with changes at a distinct collection of DNA methylation sites, the underlying biological pathways were surprisingly similar. More than 70% of the affected pathways were shared across all 10 diets. These processes help regulate essential functions such as cellular structure, communication between cells, and metabolism. They also play important roles in aging and the development of chronic diseases. The researchers identified some differences that reflected the specific goals of individual diets. For example, the DASH diet was associated with pathways related to heart health, while the MIND diet, which was developed to support brain health, showed distinct associations with pathways involved in memory and cognitive function. "More than 70 percent of the affected biological pathways were shared across all diets. These involve cell structure, cell signaling and metabolism -- processes central to aging and chronic disease. Therefore, it is understandable that the dietary patterns we examined were all linked with a slowing of biological aging," says Tavares. "A few pathways were diet-specific, and they matched each diet's main objectives: heart-related pathways were unique to the DASH diet, and pathways related to cognition and memory were unique to the so-called MIND diet, which aims to support brain health. You don't need a perfect diet -- that may be the most practical message here. But moving forward, the diet-specific pathways point to future research on targeted dietary interventions. This could be helpful in designing targeted health recommendations." Materials provided by DZNE - German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases . Note: Content may be edited for style and length. top.title: A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
top.summary: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.
top.text: Researchers at the University of Vermont have discovered a surprising pattern in human language that challenges a scientific theory widely accepted for more than 70 years. Their findings suggest that the meaning of words is shaped by something more fundamental than emotion: our understanding of power, danger, and order. The study, published in Science Advances , introduces a new approach called "ousiometrics," which uses mathematical methods to measure the essential meaning of language. Its most striking finding is that the words people use show a consistent and widespread preference for safety over danger. This hidden safety bias could transform how researchers study language, understand human behavior, and develop artificial intelligence systems that interpret what people say and write. Since the 1950s, much of the scientific understanding of word meaning has relied on a framework developed through pioneering research by psychologist Charles Osgood and others. Known as the VAD model, it describes meaning through three emotional dimensions: valence (positive vs. negative), arousal (excited vs. calm), and dominance (controlling vs. submissive). This approach became influential in psychology, linguistics, and artificial intelligence, particularly in systems designed to identify the emotional tone of written language. However, the University of Vermont researchers found evidence that this long-established model overlooks important aspects of how meaning is organized. Their analysis examined billions of individual uses of more than 20,000 words across a wide range of real-world texts. Using advanced computational techniques, the team identified a different underlying structure. They found that the three dimensions in the traditional VAD model are not independent of one another, as previously assumed. Instead, their results indicate that word meaning can be more effectively described through three separate dimensions: power (weak vs. powerful), danger (safe vs. dangerous), and structure (ordered vs. chaotic). The research, supported by the US National Science Foundation, Google, MassMutual, and other funders, found that this new framework accounted for more than 90% of the variation in measured word meaning. The traditional VAD approach explained approximately 72%. That improvement could be especially important as large language models, automated content moderation, and other AI technologies increasingly depend on understanding human communication. One of the study's most unexpected discoveries emerged when the researchers examined how words actually appear in everyday communication. Across books, news reporting, social media, and spoken language, words associated with safety appeared much more frequently than those associated with danger. This finding offers a new explanation for a familiar phenomenon called the Pollyanna principle, which describes the tendency for human language to lean toward positive rather than negative words. For decades, researchers generally interpreted this pattern as evidence that people favor positive emotional expressions. The new analysis suggests that something more fundamental may be responsible. According to the researchers, the apparent preference for positivity largely reflects an underlying preference for safety. "The Pollyanna principle's positivity bias," the study concludes. "is, in fact, a one-dimensional projection of an underlying safety bias." "This is a big observation that comes out of this work," said Peter Dodds, director of the UVM's Complex Systems Institute and senior author of the study. "Expressions of safety are crucial to all language." The discovery raises an intriguing possibility: the structure of human language may reflect evolutionary pressures associated with staying alive. From this perspective, words do more than communicate feelings. They also help people recognize threats, evaluate uncertainty, establish trust, and coordinate actions with others. Being able to distinguish between safety and danger is essential to survival. The researchers suggest that this basic human priority may also influence how meaning is organized in language. Throughout daily life, people constantly exchange information about whether individuals, places, situations, and behaviors are threatening or safe. The new findings suggest that these distinctions may be more central to communication than previously recognized. They also offer a different interpretation of why positive language is so common. Rather than simply expressing happiness or approval, many positive words may convey a sense of security, stability, or predictability. Julia Zimmerman, a postdoctoral researcher in UVM's Computational Story Lab and a co-author of the study, said the three newly identified dimensions reflect experiences that are fundamental to human life. "Power, danger, and structure," she said, "are relevant to every person that's ever lived." Researchers have also long recognized that people tend to favor language associated with goodness and low aggression. The team argues that these familiar tendencies may arise from the same deeper pattern. "We now understand," the team writes, that these are "shadows of an underlying linguistic safety bias." Although the results are consistent with a possible connection between language and survival, they do not establish that evolutionary pressures directly caused the safety bias. The findings have implications that extend well beyond linguistics. Many artificial intelligence systems use sentiment analysis to determine whether language expresses positive, negative, or neutral feelings. Some approaches also draw on the traditional VAD framework to measure emotional meaning. If that framework does not fully capture the underlying structure of language, systems built around it could overlook important distinctions in what people communicate. The researchers suggest that incorporating power, danger, and structure could eventually help AI models interpret language more accurately and explain their assessments more clearly. This may be particularly useful when analyzing trust, risk, and decision-making. In linguistics, the findings offer a different way to understand the foundations of meaning. Instead of treating emotional tone as the primary organizing principle, the new framework emphasizes distinctions related to strength, safety, and predictability. Psychology could also be affected. A different set of fundamental dimensions could encourage researchers to reconsider how some of those findings are interpreted. The discovery may also interest neuroscientists. top.title: Wireless neural chip tracks brain changes in real time after Alzheimer's drug administration
top.summary: A joint research team led by KAIST has used a small, implantable neural chip to wirelessly monitor real-time changes in a neurotransmitter involved in memory and learning after an Alzheimer's drug has been administered. In miniature pigs (minipigs), the team observed an increase in the neurotransmitter signal following drug administration, followed by a gradual return to baseline. The technology could help researchers assess how drugs act in the brain and develop stimulation methods that adapt to the brain's response.

top.title: Heart drug combo reduces kidney damage in septic shock surgery, major trial finds
top.summary: A simple adjustment to drugs given during operations for septic shock could prevent thousands of patients from suffering kidney damage, according to the results of a major trial now published in JAMA. Scientists from the University of Southampton working with experts from Zhejiang University School of Medicine in China discovered that combining the medications dobutamine and norepinephrine during surgery can significantly lower the risk of acute kidney injury.

top.title: Omega-3 EPA linked to longer survival after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases
top.summary: Patients assigned to receive high-dose eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), an omega-3 fatty acid, before and after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases had longer overall survival than those assigned to receive placebo, according to results of the phase 3 EMT2 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026, held in Madrid Oct. 23–27.

top.title: Fructose slows liver tumors in mice when key sugar-processing gene is missing, may lead to new treatments
top.summary: Fructose is an important nutrient that, despite having a chemical structure very similar to that of glucose, is metabolized very differently in the body. Research into fructose metabolism and its regulation of metabolism in the human body has in recent years become a frontier topic in the life sciences and medicine. A new study led by researchers at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) has found that in the specific metabolic context of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), dietary fructose does not fuel tumor growth. Instead, it can suppress it, revealing a previously unknown anticancer mechanism.

top.title: The degree of obesity may influence the outcomes of acute pancreatitis
top.summary: In acute pancreatitis, mild obesity might more than double the odds of vital organ failure, according to an international study by researchers at Semmelweis University analyzing data from more than 2,200 patients. The study, published in the journal Pancreatology, found that patients with obesity may have more than three times the odds of developing severe acute pancreatitis compared with patients of normal weight. Experts therefore emphasize that even gradual or smaller weight loss might reduce the odds of severe complications.

top.title: Report indicates water, food and power at risk by strong El Niño
top.summary: Rainfall reductions of up to 80% and torrential precipitation leading to severe flooding and landslides are the expected consequences across different areas of Latin America and the Caribbean from the impact of the El Niño phenomenon in 2027, according to a report co-authored by the General Secretariat of the Organization of American States (OAS), which urges member states to strengthen prevention and preparedness during the final months of 2026.

top.title: Your brain maps out numbers, including integers and fractions
top.summary: From learning to count to solving complex calculations, math requires an inherent organization of information. A team of researchers led by Stanislas Dehaene, Ph.D., and Daniela Valério, Ph.D., at the INSERM-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit (Unicog) Lab in France took dynamic brain scans of adults presented with fractions and integers. Their findings, published on Oct. 22 in the journal PLOS Biology, revealed a map of brain activity that underlies how we arrange numerical information.

top.title: Mental health support for parents after pediatric intensive care may modestly reduce PTSD and depressive symptoms
top.summary: Admission to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) can have lasting psychological effects on both children receiving treatment and their parents. To investigate the effects of psychosocial interventions on parents' emotional health, researchers searched five major academic databases for studies published through January 2026 and analyzed eight randomized controlled trials evaluating psychosocial interventions in parents of children admitted to the PICU. The interventions included visits to follow-up clinics, psychological screening with referral, telephone-based psychoeducation, palliative care consultations and acceptance and commitment therapy delivered via videoconference. top.title: Gut microbiome may help explain why sleep improvement varies after hydrogen supplementation
top.summary: A Hiroshima University–led clinical trial found that hydrogen supplementation did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with a placebo; however, exploratory analyses suggest that differences in the abundance of hydrogen-producing gut bacteria may be associated with individual differences in sleep-related responses.

top.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
top.summary: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts.

top.title: Elections are more predictable than they look
top.summary: As politics in America become more polarized and each voting cycle seems more fraught than the last, a common narrative in the media is that each election is unique and increasingly unpredictable. But new research shows that congressional elections follow strong statistical patterns, even when individual races produce surprises.

top.title: Potatoes could be the secret to better plant-based meat, say food scientists
top.summary: Potatoes could hold the key to making better gluten-free plant-based meat, according to a new study.

top.title: Can we really predict the future? Over one million forecasts offer clues, not certainty
top.summary: Can crowds of people trading on what they believe will happen collectively predict the future? A new Tel Aviv University study of more than 1 million forecasts suggests that they often come remarkably close. But when it comes to certain events, from international conflicts to elections, the odds may tell a different story.

top.title: Fossils from brickworks reveal new dinosaur species that roamed England's wetlands 125 million years ago
top.summary: More than 25 years after it was first discovered, a new species and genus of dinosaur have been named from the fossil collections cared for by the Natural History Museum. Paludohadros proudlovii was discovered at wienerberger's Ewhurst brick and roof tile works (Ewhurst Works) in Surrey in 2001 and subsequently donated to the Natural History Museum. It was a member of the iguanodontians—a group of dinosaurs known for their charismatic thumb spikes.

top.title: Can cats really thrive on vegan diets? Professor Andrew Knight responds to critics
top.summary: In response to a recent article on vegan diets for cats, Phys.org received numerous messages from concerned readers. People raised a lot of concerns, mainly arguing that cats are obligate carnivores and that vegan diets could be very harmful to their health. Now, we have collected all these comments, questions and concerns and asked the researcher behind the original paper to address them. Andrew Knight, Veterinary Professor of Animal Welfare and Associate Professor at Murdoch University School of Veterinary Medicine, offers his response below.

top.title: 121-million-year-old fossils suggest Longipteryx had no tail feathers
top.summary: Around 121 million years ago, somewhere in modern northeastern China, an early bird took to the skies. If you drew its silhouette, you'd notice something was missing. Unlike any bird alive today, it had no tail feathers.

top.title: Marine molecule may help combat 'brain-eating' amoeba
top.summary: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a parasitic disease that causes the rapid deterioration of brain tissue, is one of the most lethal infections known, with a fatality rate exceeding 97%. Caused by the free-living amoeba Naegleria fowleri (N. fowleri), the disease progresses with devastating speed, often leaving patients with only a few days to respond to treatment.

top.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
top.summary: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.
top.text: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation. And while vaccines are important, many of the health problems most likely to derail a trip cannot be prevented with a vaccine: Diarrhea, respiratory infections, motion sickness and flare-ups of existing medical conditions are all common – and none of them can be headed off with a shot. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that between 43% and 79% of travelers to low- and middle-income countries become ill during or after their trip, although most of those illnesses are mild. As an infectious diseases physician who specializes in travel and tropical medicine, I counsel many patients before they leave the country and care for them when they come home sick. A good pretravel visit to the doctor should end with more than a list of shots. You should know which illnesses you could encounter on your itinerary, which symptoms you can reasonably handle yourself, which medicines to carry and how to use them, and which warning signs mean it is time to find a doctor. Infectious disease risks abroad are constantly shifting. A good healthcare provider who specializes in travel and geographic medicine keeps up with these developments so that the advice you get reflects what is happening now, not last year. Since early 2025, South America has seen new yellow fever outbreaks that redrew long-standing risk maps and an unusual hantavirus cluster that spread from person to person aboard a cruise ship . Cases of dengue fever worldwide roughly doubled in a single year , and another tropical disease – chikungunya – also flared in new places, including the largest outbreak ever recorded in China . Fiji declared a fast-growing HIV outbreak . And common respiratory viruses, from influenza to COVID-19, continue to circulate all over the world. In my own clinical research with colleagues, we have seen travelers who returned to the U.S. with serious – and occasionally fatal – infections, such as malaria and hepatitis , often after dangerous delays in recognizing what was wrong. Travel health advice is not one-size-fits-all. A week at a Caribbean resort, a safari in East Africa and a month trekking in Nepal carry very different risks. Even the likely cause of a fever changes with the destination. Dengue is a leading concern after travel in much of Latin America and Asia, while malaria is especially important in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and typhoid and paratyphoid fever loom largest in South Asia. What you do matters, too – freshwater swimming, visiting caves, animal contact, hiking and staying in remote areas each add their own hazards . So bring your actual itinerary to the appointment. Tell your doctor not just which countries you’ll visit, but whether you’ll be in cities or the countryside, what you plan to do, how high you’ll go, how long you’ll stay and how easily you could reach a reliable hospital. For minor illnesses, you can plan to treat yourself. Travelers’ diarrhea is the best example of such an illness. Depending on the destination and season, it affects an estimated 10% to 40% of travelers during the first two weeks of a trip. Most cases clear up on their own within a few days, but having a plan makes a real difference. Ask your doctor what to do if diarrhea develops. Oral rehydration salts help replace fluids when losses are heavy. Loperamide , an over-the-counter antidiarrheal, can reduce how often and how urgently you need a bathroom, but it should not be used on its own when diarrhea comes with a fever or blood in the stool. Depending on your destination and medical history, your doctor may also give you an antibiotic to carry and use only for moderate or severe diarrhea. When it comes to treatments you’ll be administering yourself, it’s as important to ask your doctor when to use each medicine as it is to have the drugs on hand. Antibiotics have side effects, can leave you carrying drug-resistant bacteria and contribute to antibiotic resistance worldwide – so they are best saved for the episodes that truly need them. The same logic applies to other predictable problems. Someone prone to seasickness on a planned boat trip might discuss meclizine or a scopolamine patch . A traveler flying straight into a high-altitude city such as Cusco, Peru, or La Paz, Bolivia, might discuss acetazolamide, a prescription medicine that helps the body acclimatize and roughly halves the risk of altitude sickness during rapid ascents. A basic travel health kit keeps a small problem from becoming a big one. The contents depend on the traveler and the trip, but useful items include pain and fever medicine, bandages, antiseptic, oral rehydration salts , loperamide , antihistamine and anything prescribed specifically for the trip. People with chronic conditions should pack enough of their regular medications for the entire trip, plus extra in case of delays. Keep medicines in their original labeled containers, carry them in your hand luggage rather than checked bags, and consider bringing a copy of your prescriptions written with the drugs’ generic names. Replacing a medication abroad can be harder than you expect. Drugs may have different names, formulations or availability in other countries, and counterfeit or low-quality medicines remain a real problem in some places. Some medications that are routine in the U.S. are restricted or banned elsewhere. Insulin, injectable drugs, controlled substances and anything that needs refrigeration will require extra planning. Travel medicine is full of remedies with better reputations than evidence. Ginger is often recommended for motion sickness, but studies have produced mixed results . Acupressure wristbands for motion sickness do not outperform placebos . And despite their popularity, probiotics are not recommended for preventing travelers’ diarrhea , as their efficacy is still unknown. Coca leaves and coca tea are widely used for altitude symptoms in the Andes, but there is no strong evidence that they prevent altitude illness – and the same is true of garlic, ginkgo and vitamin E. “ Natural” does not mean effective , or even harmless, particularly when a supplement interacts with a prescription drug . Perhaps the most important part of any plan is recognizing when self-care is no longer appropriate. Seek medical attention for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, difficulty breathing, confusion, severe abdominal pain or an illness that is rapidly getting worse. Bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with a significant fever calls for medical care rather than simply taking an antidiarrheal and carrying on with your trip. At high altitudes, shortness of breath while resting, confusion, or difficulty walking a straight line are warning signs. Severe altitude illness is treated by descending and getting medical care – another cup of coca tea is not an adequate substitute. Fever after travel to an area where malaria is common deserves special attention. Malaria can turn deadly within hours, so get evaluated promptly and make sure the clinician knows where you have been. Some travel-related infections surface weeks or even months after you get home , which is why your travel history stays relevant long after your suitcase is unpacked. I encourage travelers to make a medical contingency plan. Ask yourself: If my flight home were canceled and I had to stay abroad another week, would I have enough medication? If I developed diarrhea tomorrow, would I know what to take? If I spiked a fever, would I know when and where to seek care? International travel will never be risk-free. But preparing for the problems most likely to happen can keep a manageable illness from becoming a medical emergency.

top.title: Decoding the loopy physics of hula hooping with high-tech earthquake sensors
top.summary: Hula hooping may be literal child's play, but as it turns out, the physics behind the gym-class staple is so complicated that scientists have spent decades trying to understand how the hula hoop defies gravity.

top.title: Are 'mega-Earths' real? Stellar activity may explain these oversized rocky worlds
top.summary: A new study suggests that some of the heaviest rocky planets ever reported may not be as heavy as they look. These so-called 'mega-Earths,' rocky planets weighing more than about 10 Earths, could be an illusion created by activity on their host stars. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 8.

top.title: Who should have a say in which species are saved? The California condor offers lessons for a global biodiversity treaty

top.text: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. Today, after decades of coordinated efforts and millions of dollars spent on captive breeding and reintroduction efforts, more than 300 condors have been restored to their natural environment. It was a victory for the species’ survival, yet this triumph was contested at nearly every step of the way. Conservationists fought bitterly over whether trapping every bird should be considered rescue or surrender. Critics argued that the cost was better spent on other threatened species. Rural communities in Utah and Arizona raised concerns about federal land-use restrictions . Hunting groups such as the National Rifle Association opposed bans on lead ammunition, a leading cause of condor deaths . The condor’s comeback illustrates several questions that governments and conservation organizations grapple with today, including which species get funded and who bears the costs. These are some of the questions being discussed at the U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity conference , being held Oct. 19-30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia. In 2022, countries worldwide adopted an agreement at that year’s biodiversity conference to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework . It includes goals to raise US$200 billion a year from public and private sources around the world by 2030 to conserve and manage at least 30% of the world’s land, coastal areas and oceans, stop human-caused extinctions and help struggling species survive. The agreement itself doesn’t choose which species to save, but its rules are designed to shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. Saving a species like the condor affects local communities and businesses whose activities have put those species at risk. Without local buy-in, pouring money into recovery efforts can fail, yet local communities are often left out of the discussions. An estimated 1 million species are currently threatened with extinction worldwide, and early assessments suggest the world is falling short on most of the agreement’s global biodiversity targets . Because resources are limited, conservationists must weigh trade-offs in deciding which species to protect and how. Should they fund expensive rescue efforts for a species close to extinction, or interventions likely to help multiple species at once? Or maybe they should protect organisms that are unique to a specific geographic region or a species that sustains local livelihoods. Some species are valued for what they do for humanity, such as pollinating crops or purifying water, known as ecosystem services . Honeybees, for example, pollinate over $15 billion worth of crops in the U.S. alone each year. Others hold cultural and spiritual significance, as the condor does for the Yurok Tribe in California. Many conservationists argue that living species possess an inherent right to exist independent of their usefulness to human beings. Getting support for measures to save charismatic species can be easier than for others, however. Think of Greenpeace’s “save the whales” campaign or the World Wildlife Fund’s panda logo. A panda’s adorable face can help pay for its protection and potentially the protection of its surrounding habitat , helping other species living there. A 2025 study examined more than 14,000 species-focused conservation projects from 1992 to 2016. Five mammal groups – primates, carnivores, whales, elephants and rhinos – received 86% of available funding , despite accounting for only one-third of threatened mammal projects. Plants and invertebrates, which are crucial for pollination, nutrient cycling and sustaining food webs, received only 6.6% of the financial backing. Conservation groups and economists at the Paulson Institute estimate that the world needs to spend an additional $1.3 trillion annually on biodiversity conservation and restoration to stop and reverse biodiversity loss. At the 2026 biodiversity conference, delegates will also take up another question that can make or break species recovery: When conservation affects local people, who pays and who gets a say? While conservationists celebrated efforts to return wolves to Europe over the past two decades, some farmers lost livestock to these predators and faced higher costs to protect their flocks. Current European Union funding programs help support livestock protection , but farmers’ ability to shape wolf recovery is part of the story too. Conservation can go terribly wrong if local communities aren’t consulted during planning. In the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a protected area in Tanzania, the Maasai have fought for years against government orders that they leave the land they have lived on for generations in the name of lion conservation. In March 2026, two presidential commissions recommended that the evictions continue in order to protect wildlife, in a process that included few Maasai , Indigenous peoples’ advocates at the Oakland Institute reported. Protecting vulnerable species often means also supporting the communities living alongside them. At the last round of biodiversity talks in 2024, countries created a permanent advisory body to bring Indigenous peoples and local communities’ knowledge and decisions into the treaty’s decisions. At this year’s conference, known as COP17, they must agree on how that advisory body will operate, including whether these communities get a formal role in decision-making. They are also expected to adopt guidelines for how the 30% global conservation targets apply in Indigenous territories. The international agreement can’t dictate what happens on the ground, but its rules shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. That is why the debate over local consultation is at the heart of the 2026 talks. Conservation that is designed for people, rather than with them, risks losing the trust and local cooperation that makes recovery last. Two key issues at the conference involve guaranteeing that Indigenous peoples and local communities have a say in decisions on their territory, including how conservation programs are designed and how resources are allocated. The global biodiversity framework calls for a “ whole-of-society” approach , recognizing that protecting nature needs more than government action alone. But participation is not the same as decision-making power. Advocates for Indigenous groups say communities are too often consulted after priorities are set, rather than being involved in setting them. Whether the farmer paying for fencing or the Indigenous community with connections to a species helps set priorities or is only asked for input after the project has been approved shows whether consultation is genuine or not. The condor’s return shows that nearly extinct species can recover with help. But sustaining a species’ recovery requires protecting the conditions – and supporting the people – that make their survival possible. Researcher Garrett Ordonez, an environmental studies and international relations student at USC, contributed to this article.
